key_facts: **Ingrowing toenail** (onychocryptosis): the nail edge pierces the lateral fold, usually of the **big toe**.
Commonest in teenagers and young men; causes: cutting nails curved or too short, tight shoes, hyperhidrosis, involuted nails.
Stages: inflammation → infection with granulation tissue → chronic fold hypertrophy.
Cut straight across, wide shoes, soaks, lift the edge; antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis.
Recurrent: **partial nail avulsion with phenol** by podiatry (about 95% success). Diabetes or PAD: refer early.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: An **ingrowing toenail** (onychocryptosis) is penetration of the **lateral nail fold** by the edge of the nail plate, most often of the **great toe**. It is commonest in teenagers and young men.

sub: Adolescents and young adults, males more than females; also older people with thickened nails.

ul: **Causes:** cutting nails curved or too short, tight shoes, hyperhidrosis, a naturally involuted ("pincer") nail. Commonest in teenagers and young men. **Retinoids** (isotretinoin) and some EGFR inhibitors cause periungual granulation tissue that looks the same.
Nail cutting, footwear, sweaty feet, trauma, pincer nails.
Drugs: isotretinoin and EGFR inhibitors cause similar periungual granulation.
**"Cut a V in the middle of the nail"**: this does not work; cut straight across.
**"Antibiotics fix it"**: they do not remove the spike of nail.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A **spike of nail** acts as a foreign body in the nail fold.

mech.t: A sharp nail edge pierces the lateral fold, often after cutting the corner short.
The fold becomes red, swollen and painful; bacteria colonise the wound.
Continued irritation produces moist, bleeding 'proud flesh' overhanging the nail.
mech.caption: Ingrowing toenail with granulation tissue on the lateral fold; inset: nail cut straight across.

mech.t: Removing the edge and destroying that strip of matrix (phenol) stops regrowth.

ul: **Stages:** inflammation → infection with granulation tissue ("proud flesh") → chronic hypertrophy of the fold.
Pain, redness and swelling of the lateral fold; later discharge, pus and **granulation tissue** ("proud flesh") overhanging the nail.

sub: High risk of infection, ulceration and amputation: early podiatry.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. Consider X-ray only if a subungual exostosis is suspected; biopsy any atypical or non-healing granulation (amelanotic melanoma, SCC).

ul: **Acute paronychia** (see [Paronychia](condition:paronychia)): fingers more often, no nail spicule.
**Subungual exostosis**: firm bony lump under the distal nail; X-ray.
**Pyogenic granuloma** from retinoids or EGFR inhibitors (see [Pyogenic granuloma](condition:pyogenic-granuloma)).
**Amelanotic melanoma or SCC**: non-healing, atypical granulation tissue: biopsy.

**Conservative care:** cut the nail straight across, wear wide-toe-box shoes, warm salt soaks, lift the edge (cotton wisp or dental floss), use a gutter splint. Topical antiseptic. Antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis.

**Definitive:** **partial nail avulsion with phenol matricectomy** by **podiatry**. Success is ~95% and lower recurrence than avulsion alone. Total avulsion is for recurrent or bilateral disease. Diabetes or PAD → **refer early to podiatry** (foot-protection service).

ladder.t: Cut nails **straight across**, not too short; wide-toe-box shoes. Warm salt-water soaks; lift the nail edge with a cotton wisp or dental floss; topical antiseptic.
Gutter splint or podiatry review. **Antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis.**
**Partial nail avulsion with phenol matricectomy** by podiatry (~95% success); total avulsion for recurrent or bilateral disease.

refer.t: Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease or neuropathy with an ingrowing or infected toenail: **podiatry / foot-protection service**.
Recurrent ingrowing toenail despite conservative care: podiatry for partial avulsion and phenol.
Atypical or non-healing 'granulation' tissue: biopsy to exclude amelanotic melanoma or SCC.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease or neuropathy: **refer early to podiatry** (foot-protection service).
Spreading cellulitis or systemic upset.
Atypical or non-healing granulation tissue: biopsy to exclude malignancy.
Paronychia, cellulitis, osteomyelitis (rare).
Recurrence after simple avulsion.
Mild cases settle with conservative care; phenol matricectomy rarely recurs.
Cut toenails **straight across**, not too short.
Partial avulsion **plus phenol** matricectomy has the lowest recurrence.
